Q: How do i get the list of Reviewers for a pull request using Github api? A:

If you want to know when the review requests were made to a PR, you can call:

GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number}/timeline

From there you can filter by event=review_requested

The difference with the above solutions is that it does return an empty response once the review is completed like /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/reviews does

Docs are here: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/reference/issues#timeline

Q: Java NIO: Ideal approach to HIgh-Speed Sequencially Streaming large binary data to a file A:

If speed is really critical, I would start with a straight forward implementation and write to a ramdisk. Don't prematurely optimize. First write something that works. Then profile it if it isn't fast enough. Because where is this sequential binary data coming from? Presumably you only have to write fast enough to capture that.

Q: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class org.keycloak.KeycloakPrincipal A:

I would double, and even triple check that the object is not null. You may see in your code that you are indeed setting a SecurityContext with an Authentication that has a Principal with your specific type of KeycloackPrincipal, however if it is null, an AnonymousAuthentificationFilter will silently put a String object as the Principal. So it may look like your custom Filter is passing some checks, and properly executes, but the Principal is set by a downstream Filter.

Q: How to get canonical IANA timezone ids in javascript A:

This question was also asked here. I'm cross-posting the answer to help others in the future:

It sounds like you have four questions:

  1. Why does Temporal's definition of "primary time zone identifier" differ from the list of canonical (non-Link) zone names shown in Wikipedia's list of IANA time zone database zone names?
  2. What's a good API to fetch a list of all time zone IDs, as well as a mapping between each ID and its primary time zone identifier?
  3. Why doesn't the current Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone') API's results match the Temporal spec's definition of "primary time zone identifier" ?
  4. Why does Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone') only return canonical IDs ("primary time zone identifiers") not all IDs?

These are reasonable questions. I'll try to answer each on in order.

1. Why does Temporal's definition of "primary time zone identifier" differ from the list of canonical (non-Link) zone names shown in [Wikipedia's list of IANA time zone database zone names]

To answer, first I'll provide some historical context. For many years, long predating Temporal, JS engines have long relied on the ICU library for all time-zone-related APIs. ICU, in turn, relies on CLDR, as specified here, for the list of time zones made available to JavaScript APIs, including Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone').

CLDR has for many years followed the principle that time zones should not span country boundaries. This ensures that political changes to time zones in one country won't change the meaning of a timestamp in another country. This guideline also ensures that when showing a time zone picker in a UI, you'll have at least one entry for each country, which is helpful for developers who, for example, might not want to force users from Norway or the Netherlands to pick the time zone for Germany, a choice with quite a bit of historical baggage.

The IANA TZDB used to follow the same guideline, but over the last decade its maintainers chose to merge all zones that have had the same rules since 1970, even across country boundaries. This choice was very controversial, and resulted in, among others, the Joda Time maintainer forking tzdb to undo these changes. The TZDB maintainers eventually added new build options to TZDB that would add back the IDs that were merged, so that users like Joda who preferred things as they were could still use TZDB without forking.

Personally I agree with CLDR and Joda's guidelines, because of how time zone IDs are used in many applications as persisted identifiers that may refer to future timestamps. It'd be bad enough if Norwegian or Dutch or Icelandic users need to pick another country's time zone. What's even worse is if a political decision in Berlin or Abidjan changes the meaning of a future timestamp in a completely different country. Imagine a Norwegian software developer having to tell their customers that a change in Berlin broke their recurring calendar invites!

But regardless of my personal opinion, an important tenet of JavaScript is that newly-introduced features should avoid breaking existing code. Adopting the default build options of TZDB would be a fairly significant breaking change, so would never have been approved by the TC39 committee that controls the evolution of JavaScript, and that all changes (including Temporal) need to be approved by. So, honestly, we didn't really have a choice when building Temporal: we needed to align with CLDR's definition of which zones were canonical vs. not, or we never would have been permitted to add Temporal to JavaScript.

Anyway, in the Temporal specification, the definition of primary time zone identifier is really just a reverse-engineering of CLDR's methods for deciding which TZDB changes should be followed (e.g. merges inside countries, like America/Montreal => America/Toronto) and which should be ignored, like Europe/Oslo => Europe/Berlin.

You can look at the spec text for AvailableNamedTimeZoneIdentifiers to see exactly how this reverse-engineering is defined.

2. What's a good API to fetch a list of all time zone IDs, as well as a mapping between each ID and its primary time zone identifier?

You are correct that there are lower-level APIs that can provide lists of time zone IDs in more detail. You can use ICU4C (a C++ API) or ICU4J (the corresponding Java API) to enumerate IDs, including which ones are canonical vs. not. Note that the ICU's default "what is canonical?" answer is by default constrained by ICU's historical insistence of never changing the canonical identifier for a zone. So Asia/Calcutta, despite being out-of-date by more than a decade, is still returned by the getCanonicalID API. That's why there's a new getIanaId API that returns the modern IDs.

Note that these ICU APIs are just a thin wrapper over the underlying CLDR data found here: https://github.com/unicode-org/cldr/blob/main/common/bcp47/timezone.xml. For each zone in that file, the first ID in the alias attribute is the canonical one (according to ICU), and if there's an iana attribute present, that's the one that's primary according to Temporal, not the first alias.

So if all you're looking for is the list of zones and their canonical-ness, you can use that API or that file. You can also use the new ICU4X Rust API. BTW, this is the API that Chrome's implementation of Temporal uses.

3. Why doesn't the current Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone') API's results match the Temporal spec's definition of "primary time zone identifier" ?

The current plan is that existing Intl APIs will switch to Temporal's definition of primary time zone identifier when Temporal is officially merged into the ECMAScript specification when Temporal reaches Stage 4 in the TC39 process. This just happened a few weeks ago (March 2026) but things move slowly in browser-land and this change is not guaranteed.

The most significant change will be that outdated IDs like Asia/Calcutta and Europe/Kiev will be replaced by modern IDs like Asia/Kolkata and Europe/Kyiv, as discussed in the Time Zone Canonicalization proposal (caveat: it's 3 years old so some parts have been superseded by later Temporal changes). Your "Indiana/Indianapolis" vs. "America/Indiana/Indianapolis" example will also be resolved, as will a few tens of other cases like that.

In addition, there are other less significant differences between JS engines that may or may not be resolved. For example, Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone').includes('UTC') will return true on Safari but false on Chrome. This is because although JS engines are strongly encouraged to follow the ECMAScript spec, there are still individual people at Google, Apple, Mozilla, and others who have to make the actual code changes required, and there is not yet consensus among those opinionated individuals about whetheer "UTC" belongs in a time zone picker or not. Hopefully we will be able to get that consensus in the future.

Note that all the Etc/* IDs have the same issue: Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone').filter(z => z.startsWith('Etc/')) returns 26 zones in Firefox (Etc/GMT+1", "Etc/GMT+10", "Etc/GMT+11", ...) but zero on Chrome. Hopefully we'll resolve this in the future too.

4. Why does Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone') only return canonical IDs ("primary time zone identifiers") not all IDs?

The current answer to this question is straightforward: because since its inception this API has only returned canonical IDs, and JS generally refuses to change the behavior of existing APIs to avoid breaking existing code.

But the logical follow-up question is: why was this decision made to only include canonical IDs when this API was first introduced?

The answer here is also straightforward: because the primary use case of this API was to power a time zone dropdown UI pickers showing of localized time zone names. Given that obsolete time zone aliases like GB will yield the same localized name as the modern name Europe/London, the designers of the Intl.supportedValuesOf('timeZone') API realized that showing duplicate localized names in a UI picker would be a bad user experience and would be confusing for end users, so they opted to only return canonical IDs.

Temporal's concept of time zones (more specifically, how to merge together different time zone aliases differently from how the default build options of TZDB do) takes a lot of inspiration from CLDR's concept of time zones, which is based on which ones produce unique display names. "Europe/Berlin" and "Europe/Oslo" could produce different display names in some locales, so they should not be merged, even though TZDB links them. However, legacy things like "US/Arizona" should definitely be merged with their modern counterparts like "America/Phoenix".

It's a reasonable question whether an additional API should be added to provide all time zone IDs, not just the canonical ones. The bar for adding new JS APIs is very high (for example, despite the strong support for Temporal on TC39 for more than 7 years, we still had to strip out about 1/3 of the APIs in Temporal before Google was be OK with it!) so it's probably unlikely that an all-aliases API could get consensus from TC39. But you're welcome to try! A first step could be asking over in the ECMA 402 repo.

Q: Why are Relational Algebra, Tuple Relational Calculus, and Domain Relational Calculus used in DB management, given SQL? A:

SQL is a (perverted) mix of relational algebra, tuple calculus and domain calculus. So one is using notions from all three when one is using SQL. So SQL certainly thinks it's helpful to "use all three".

Moreover, these are all simpler than SQL and explaining SQL and reasoning about SQL queries is simplest in terms of them. They predate SQL, so SQL is otherwise irrelevant to "using all three".

The relational calculus notations are styled after predicate calculus, which involves expressions using AND, OR, NOT and EXISTS/FORALL and is the precise notation used in engineering (including software engineering), science (including computer/information science) and mathematics (including logic).

When relational algebra was introduced it was thought by Codd that a predicate calculus style notation would be clearer than an algebra style notation. (SQL was introduced because it was thought by its design team that SQL would be clearer than either.) It turns out both algebra & calculus are useful. (As SQL demonstrates by using parts of both.)

Difference between Relational Algebra and Relational Calculus

Does an empty SQL table have a superkey? Does every SQL table have one?

Q: What is a greenlet? A:

A greenlet is block of sequential frames on the CPython C stack that can be swapped out to the heap.

This is the general fundamental building block needed to implement coroutines.

The native coroutine implementation in Python does not save C frames to the heap. It's designed to not have important data on the C stack, and then uses send() and yield [from] to unwind/rebuild each frame of the C stack as you suspend/resume the coroutine. The downside to this is that you need to unnecessarily spam chains of yield from's throughout your codebase, and suffer the all the overhead of the stack unwinding/rebuilding. Overall, native python generators are pretty weak in terms of performance and syntactic support.

Stackless Python avoids using the C stack for Python function calls all together (because if there isn’t any useful context, what's the point?). All the needed context is stored in Python frames (which has the Python stack, instruction pointer (IP), local variables, return frames, etc.). PyPy contains Stackless Python, which is part of the reasons its performance is so much better.

Greenlets were inspired by Stackless Python. As an extension module for CPython, the C stack is still used for Python function calls, but you can swap out blocks of frames (this block "is" the coroutine/greenlet) to the heap on demand. Now you can mix execution of coroutines however you'd like to achieve your goals. This way you can get something better than generators in CPython without having to completely switch to PyPy.
